say: You go straight from the dinner table to the sofa, and your blood sugar gets the whole evening to itself.
Let's get you off that sofa.
Your body was built to walk, not to lie on the sofa after dinner like a python digesting a goat.
In a study of forty-one adults with type 2 diabetes, everyone walked thirty minutes a day, either in one go or as ten minutes after each main meal.
With the same thirty minutes, walking after meals made the rise in their blood sugar after eating about twelve percent smaller, and after dinner, twenty-two percent smaller.
It was the same walk, with better timing.
These are short studies, so call it a good habit, not a cure.
So after your main meals, especially dinner, walk for about ten minutes: around the block, to the shop, or with the dog.
The dishes will wait. They always do.
If you take insulin or another diabetes medicine that can make your blood sugar drop too low, ask your doctor how extra walking fits with your doses.
Let's get you back to factory settings.

reynolds2016: Reynolds AN et al. Advice to walk after meals is more effective for lowering postprandial glycaemia in type 2 diabetes mellitus than advice that does not specify timing: a randomised crossover study. Diabetologia 2016: 41 adults with type 2 diabetes (mean age 60); 30 min a day either at any time or as 10 min after each main meal (the same total); post-meal glucose (iAUC) 12% lower with after-meal walking (ratio 0.88, 0.78 to 0.99), 22% lower after the evening meal (0.78, 0.67 to 0.91)
